  "title": "Miscalibration-Triggered Adaptive Generation via Logit-Level Intervention",
  "core_problem": "Overconfident hallucinations—where an LLM asserts falsehoods with high verbal confidence despite internal epistemic uncertainty—are the most user-deceptive failure mode. Standard factuality metrics (FActScore, TruthfulQA) treat all hallucinations equally, but overconfident ones are disproportionately harmful because users cannot distinguish them from accurate claims. Existing inference-time mitigation methods each have critical limitations: (1) activation steering (Ji et al., TA-ITI) is undermined by Endogenous Steering Resistance in larger models; (2) external-monitor approaches (Monitoring Decoding) require expensive reference models; (3) density-estimation approaches (PC-LDCD) detect general factual anomalies but do not specifically target the verbal-internal mismatch signal that marks overconfident hallucinations, and remain unvalidated beyond 8B models or on long-form generation; (4) recent calibration-aware methods (CAG, CURE) require model fine-tuning, precluding deployment on frozen models; and (5) post-generation approaches (CSS) cannot prevent overconfident hallucinations from being generated and consumed during streaming. No existing work combines a miscalibration-specific trigger with ESR-immune logit-level intervention for graded, during-generation control of overconfident hallucinations using only internal signals.",
  "opportunity": "Ji et al. (EMNLP 2025 Outstanding) proved verbal-internal uncertainty mismatch predicts hallucinations better than uncertainty alone, but only demonstrated offline binary activation intervention on short-form QA—now undermined by ESR in larger models. Monitoring Decoding (ACL 2025 Findings) proved selective token-level intervention during generation works (+15.4% TruthfulQA) but requires an expensive external reference model. PC-LDCD (arXiv 2605.05953) proved internal-signal-triggered selective contrastive decoding achieves SOTA on TruthfulQA for ≤8B models (True+Info 0.78 on Qwen3-4B) but targets general density anomalies rather than the specific overconfident-hallucination signal, and is untested on long-form generation. Concurrently, Guo et al. (arXiv 2604.05306) showed training models to emit explicit uncertainty markers improves calibration, and CAG (arXiv 2605.01749) improved long-form factuality by up to 13% via calibration-aware generation—but both require fine-tuning. CSS (arXiv 2604.17487) achieves training-free specificity control via post-generation claim backoff but cannot intervene during streaming generation. Tao et al. (arXiv 2601.10960) independently validated that training-free logit-level intervention achieves +47% accuracy for controllable generation attributes, confirming the paradigm. The opportunity: combine the miscalibration trigger signal (specifically targeting overconfident hallucinations) with ESR-immune logit-level intervention for training-free, during-generation control with graded severity—using only internal model signals, no reference model, no fine-tuning—filling the gap left between training-based calibration methods and post-generation correction approaches.",
  "landscape": "Ji et al. (EMNLP 2025) showed ~30% reduction in overconfident hallucinations via linear activation intervention on the VUF direction, but only for short-form answers with binary logic, and ESR (arXiv 2602.06941, Feb 2026) demonstrates that Llama-3.3-70B actively resists activation steering mid-generation. Monitoring Decoding (Chang et al., ACL 2025 Findings) monitors factuality during generation using a reference model's probability distribution, triggering tree-based resampling of flagged tokens (+15.4% TruthfulQA with 5.7x latency); requires a larger reference model (70B for 7B target). PC-LDCD (Nielsen et al., arXiv 2605.05953, May 2026) trains PCNet over the residual stream to detect hallucinations as geometric anomalies, triggering selective contrastive decoding; achieves SOTA TruthfulQA (True+Info up to 0.78 on Qwen3-4B) on 3/4 models (1B-8B), but targets general factual-error signals rather than overconfident hallucinations specifically, and is untested on long-form generation or models >8B. DoLa (ICLR 2024) contrasts logits across layers (+12-17% TruthfulQA). ActLCD (EMNLP 2025) extends DoLa with RL-optimized layer selection (+19.81% TruthfulQA). LoGU (ACL 2025) adds hedging via SFT+DPO training (requires fine-tuning). Simple Factuality Probes (obalcells et al., EMNLP 2025 Findings) detect entity-level hallucinations with AUC 0.87-0.90 across Llama, Qwen-2.5, Gemma, and Mistral families, with cross-model transfer within 0.02-0.04 AUC of same-model performance, but offer no intervention mechanism. **Concurrent work (2026)**: CAG (arXiv 2605.01749) improves long-form factuality by up to 13% via exploration-commitment decoupling but requires multi-stage fine-tuning. CURE (arXiv 2604.12046) achieves +39.9% claim-level accuracy on biographies via reasoning calibration but requires training. CSS (arXiv 2604.17487) achieves 0.913 overcommitment-aware utility on LongFact via training-free post-generation claim-level specificity backoff, but operates post-hoc, cannot intervene during streaming generation, and does not use internal uncertainty signals. CLC (arXiv 2502.19110) provides conformal guarantees on factuality-specificity tradeoff but requires fine-tuning. Logit-Level Steering (Tao et al., arXiv 2601.10960) validates training-free logit intervention for controllable generation (+47% accuracy on attribute control) but uses static score tables, not dynamic uncertainty-triggered intervention. TruthfulQA (817 questions, 38 domains) remains the standard short-form benchmark despite known saturation and contamination concerns (Turntrout 2025, Deng et al. ICLR 2025); we include it for comparability but complement with FActScore for long-form evaluation. No existing work combines: (a) miscalibration-based trigger specifically targeting overconfident hallucinations, (b) ESR-immune logit-level intervention, (c) graded action vocabulary with distinct calibration and factuality benefits, (d) training-free during-generation operation on long-form generation.",
  "approach": "We propose MisTAG (Miscalibration-Triggered Adaptive Generation), a training-free inference-time framework that monitors verbal-internal uncertainty mismatch during long-form generation and triggers ESR-immune logit-level interventions graded by mismatch severity. We explicitly separate two complementary goals: **calibration correction** (ensuring verbal confidence matches internal uncertainty, measured by OHR) and **factuality improvement** (reducing hallucinated content, measured by FActScore and TruthfulQA).\n\n**Prerequisite Validation (Days 1-2)**: Before main experiments, we train linear factuality probes on Qwen3-8B hidden states and verify: (a) AUROC ≥0.85 on held-out LongFact generations (matching obalcells et al.'s reported 0.87-0.90 for Qwen-2.5-7B), and (b) probe activation concentration at entity-bearing token spans via span-level activation analysis (computing mean probe activation for NER-tagged entity spans vs. non-entity spans). If AUROC <0.85 or entity concentration is weak, we add explicit NER-based entity gating (applying miscalibration scoring only at spaCy-detected entity boundaries) as a fallback. This validation is prerequisite: failure terminates the project early rather than producing unreliable results.\n\n**Miscalibration Detection**: At each generated token, we compute a miscalibration score as the discrepancy between (1) verbal confidence, extracted via projection onto the Verbal Uncertainty Feature direction (Ji et al.) in the residual stream at the final layer, and (2) internal epistemic uncertainty, estimated via a lightweight linear factuality probe (trained on hidden states following obalcells et al.'s methodology with span-max loss). The miscalibration score is defined as: M(t) = σ(VUF_confidence(t)) × probe_hallucination_prob(t), where high verbal confidence multiplied by high probe-estimated hallucination probability yields high miscalibration. This score naturally concentrates at entity-bearing tokens because the span-max training loss optimizes the probe to peak at the most informative token per entity span. The VUF projection and probe forward pass are computed in a single batched operation on the already-extracted hidden state at layer ⌊0.95×num_layers⌋, adding minimal overhead (two dot products: one for VUF projection, one for probe classification).\n\n**Graded Logit-Level Intervention** (ESR-immune since they operate on the output distribution post-residual-stream, not on internal activations):\n\n- *Mild mismatch (M(t) > τ_mild) → Hedge (calibration correction)*: Apply a static logit bias vector b ∈ R^|V| at the next-token prediction: log p'(v) = log p(v) + α·b(v). The bias vector b is constructed from a curated vocabulary partition: b(v) = +1 for hedge tokens (~50 tokens: 'likely', 'approximately', 'reportedly', 'possibly', 'around', 'roughly', 'perhaps', 'estimated', etc.), b(v) = -1 for assertive tokens (~30 tokens: 'definitely', 'certainly', 'clearly', 'undoubtedly', 'always', 'never', 'exactly', etc.), and b(v) = 0 otherwise. The scalar magnitude α is tuned on the validation set. **We frame this action as calibration correction, not factuality improvement**: it makes the model's verbal expression match its internal uncertainty, reducing the Overconfident Hallucination Rate (OHR). Regarding FActScore, hedging may indirectly improve precision by converting specific false claims into vaguer ones that FActScore's atomic-fact decomposition categorizes as too imprecise to verify (effectively implicit selective abstention at the claim level)—we test this hypothesis empirically rather than assuming it.\n\n- *Severe mismatch (M(t) > τ_severe) → Abstain (factuality improvement)*: Rollback generation to the last sentence boundary (discard tokens and KV-cache entries following UT-ACA's rollback mechanism), then regenerate with constrained prefix decoding that forces the replacement sentence to begin with an epistemic marker (sampled from: 'I'm not certain, but', 'It is unclear whether', 'Some sources suggest', 'This may not be accurate, but'). During regeneration, the hedge logit bias is applied (α at 2× mild level). **Anti-cascading safeguards**: (1) After any rollback, suppress severe-mismatch triggering for N_cool = 30 tokens (cooldown window), allowing the forced uncertainty prefix to establish without re-triggering; mild-mismatch hedging remains active during cooldown. (2) Maximum R_max = 3 rollbacks per generation; if exceeded, continue generation with persistent mild-level hedging for the remainder. These prevent infinite rollback loops while maintaining calibration correction.\n\n**Threshold Optimization**: We adopt a principled two-stage approach following AdaDec's data-driven philosophy. Stage 1: Fit a logistic regression boundary on validation miscalibration scores (M(t) at entity-bearing tokens) labeled by FActScore atomic-fact verification (supported=0, not-supported=1) to determine τ_mild (operating point at 80% recall of hallucinated entities) and τ_severe (operating point at 95% precision of hallucinated entities). Stage 2: Grid search over α ∈ {0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5} with hard constraints: length_reduction_ratio < 15% and Δperplexity < 5%. Validation set: ~200 long-form biography generations from FActScore's entity set, held out from evaluation. Total optimization surface: 2 thresholds (data-driven) + 1 magnitude (5-point grid) = tractable and reproducible.\n\n**Latency Benchmarking**: We measure and report per-token overhead (ms/token) and end-to-end throughput (tokens/second) for: (a) baseline greedy decoding, (b) MisTAG with detection only (no intervention), (c) MisTAG with hedge intervention, (d) MisTAG with hedge + rollback. Based on the probe architecture (single linear layer on already-extracted hidden states) and VUF projection (single dot product), we expect <5% per-token overhead for detection; rollback incurs sentence-level regeneration cost proportional to the rollback rate. We report the fraction of tokens triggering each intervention level.\n\n**Evaluation**: We evaluate primarily on Qwen3-8B (FP16, single A100 80GB). Qwen3-32B (INT8 via LLM.int8() on H100 80GB, with probes trained directly on INT8 hidden states) serves as a scaling ablation if time permits.\n\n*Benchmarks (4 axes)*: (1) **TruthfulQA** (MC1, MC2, True+Info) for short-form truthfulness and direct baseline comparison with all cited methods; (2) **FActScore biographies** for long-form factual precision, the primary evaluation of the rollback action's factuality benefit; (3) **OHR (Overconfident Hallucination Rate)**: the fraction of hallucinated atomic facts (per FActScore) where the model used assertive language without hedging markers, following Ji et al.'s annotation scheme—this is the primary metric for the calibration-correction contribution, capturing the specific failure mode that existing metrics miss; (4) **MT-Bench** for multi-turn dialogue quality preservation.\n\n*Baselines (5 primary)*: (a) Greedy/nucleus decoding, (b) DoLa contrastive decoding, (c) ActLCD, (d) PC-LDCD (reimplemented with PCNet trained on same probe training data), (e) the detect-only hallucination probe (obalcells) without intervention. *Secondary baselines (if time permits)*: (f) Ji et al.'s activation-based intervention, (g) Monitoring Decoding (using Qwen3-32B as reference for Qwen3-8B).\n\n*Ablation studies*: (i) Hedge-only vs. Rollback-only vs. full MisTAG (disentangling calibration vs. factuality contributions), (ii) Miscalibration trigger vs. probe-only trigger vs. VUF-only trigger (validating the mismatch signal), (iii) Anti-cascading ablation (with/without cooldown and max-rollback), (iv) Threshold sensitivity (varying τ_mild, τ_severe by ±1 standard deviation).\n\n*Analysis*: (a) Per-component FActScore and OHR contribution (hedge vs. rollback), (b) Hedge-FActScore interaction analysis: do hedged claims produce fewer or differently-scored atomic facts in FActScore decomposition? (c) Latency overhead analysis across intervention levels, (d) Qualitative examples of overconfident hallucinations caught vs. missed.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 4)
Issues: ["Single model family evaluation (Qwen3-8B primary, Qwen3-32B ablation) is insufficient for EMNLP. PC-LDCD tested 3 families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral), obalcells tested 4 families. Without at least one non-Qwen model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B or Mistral-7B), reviewers will question whether the miscalibration signal generalizes or is Qwen-specific.", "The hedge action's contribution to actual factuality is uncertain and inadequately justified. Boosting 'likely'/'approximately' tokens doesn't correct misinformation—it decorates it with uncertainty language. FActScore still decomposes 'approximately 1067' into a verifiable atomic fact and judges it unsupported. The proposal acknowledges this ('we test this hypothesis empirically') but if hedging only improves OHR without improving FActScore, the paper's value proposition reduces to 'we made wrong answers sound less confident'—a weaker contribution for EMNLP's Generation track.", "API costs for FActScore evaluation (requires LLM-as-judge for atomic-fact decomposition + verification per biography) and MT-Bench (LLM-judge per conversation) are not budgeted. For ~200 biographies × multiple conditions × 5 baselines, FActScore alone requires thousands of LLM API calls. This could easily add $200-500+ in API costs unaccounted in the resource estimate.", "PC-LDCD differentiation needs empirical grounding, not just theoretical argument. The claim that miscalibration trigger specifically catches overconfident hallucinations that density-anomaly detection misses is the core novelty claim but is untested. Without a head-to-head comparison showing cases where PC-LDCD misses overconfident hallucinations that MisTAG catches, the 'better trigger signal' argument is hypothetical.", "OHR (Overconfident Hallucination Rate) as a primary metric is risky for venue acceptance. It is custom, unpublished, and its annotation scheme (detecting 'assertive language without hedging markers') requires validation of inter-annotator agreement or automated detection reliability. Reviewers may dismiss improvements on a self-defined metric."]
Feedback: The proposal is technically sound and addresses all round 3 feedback. The remaining gap is demonstrating that MisTAG provides value BEYOND what PC-LDCD already delivers. To reach pass threshold:

1. **Add one non-Qwen model** (Llama-3.1-8B is ideal—VUF validated on it, probes validated on Llama family, fits on A100). This is the most impactful change for EMNLP reviewers. Even if it's secondary (fewer ablations), having 2 families in the main results table is near-mandatory.

2. **Commit to a clear contribution narrative**: Frame the paper as: (a) MisTAG's miscalibration signal targets a *specific* failure mode (overconfident hallucinations) that general-purpose methods (DoLa, PC-LDCD) do not specifically address; (b) the hedge action is a *calibration* contribution (measured by OHR + ECE), not a factuality contribution; (c) the rollback action is the *factuality* contribution (measured by FActScore). This dual-contribution framing is honest and novel. Don't oversell hedging as factuality improvement.

3. **Design the PC-LDCD comparison to highlight your advantage**: Show a confusion-matrix analysis—what fraction of overconfident hallucinations does PC-LDCD miss that MisTAG catches? If M(t) triggers on cases where PCNet's density score is normal (because the model is confidently wrong in a way that looks 'on-manifold'), that's your strongest novelty evidence.

4. **Budget API costs explicitly**: Add an 'evaluation API cost' line (~$300-500 for FActScore + MT-Bench across all conditions). This is realistic and shows awareness.

5. **Validate OHR reliability**: Add a small annotation study (50-100 examples) showing that automated OHR annotation (using hedging-marker detection) agrees with human judgment at ≥0.85 Cohen's kappa. This takes <1 day and preempts the 'self-defined metric' objection.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，执行以下搜索流程：

1. **如果 reviewer 说'已有类似工作'**：
   - 搜索 reviewer 提到的论文，用 WebFetch 实际阅读
   - 搜索该论文的 cited-by，找到后续跟进工作
   - 明确你的 idea 与这些工作的差异化点——如果差异化不够，必须 pivot

2. **如果 reviewer 说'SOTA 过时'**：
   - 用 Papers With Code 查看当前排行榜
   - 搜索过去 6 个月的最新方法
   - 更新你的 landscape 和 baseline

3. **如果 reviewer 说'可行性有问题'**：
   - 搜索类似规模实验的实际成本和时间线
   - 搜索 GitHub 上是否有可复用的实现
   - 搜索相关数据集/模型的可获取性

4. **如果 reviewer 说'novelty 不足'**：
   - 对核心方法尽量做 3-5 种不同关键词组合的搜索
   - 搜索相邻领域是否有类似思路
   - 如果确实 novelty 不足，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- Use WebSearch to find updated information if the reviewer flagged outdated claims.
- You have full freedom in how much to change:
  - Minor fix: if only specific details are wrong, correct them and keep everything else.
  - Major revision: if the approach is fundamentally flawed but the core problem is valid, you may redesign the approach entirely.
  - Pivot: if the reviewer's feedback reveals that the core problem itself is invalid (e.g., the gap no longer exists), you may propose a RELATED but substantially different idea that builds on the same research area. This is preferred over forcing a doomed idea to pass review.
- The output replaces the original idea (same tracking ID). Whether you make a small tweak or a full pivot, output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields filled.
- In the output JSON, include a "change_type" field with one of: "minor", "major", or "pivot" to indicate the scope of your changes.
- Output the revised idea as a COMPLETE JSON object (same schema as original, plus "change_type").

## 停滞提醒
这个 idea 已经经过 4 轮修订，近 3 轮的平均分从 3.2 到 3.5，没有明显改善。

请认真思考：
- 当前方向是否存在根本性的瓶颈？反复的 minor fix 是否在回避核心问题？
- 如果你认为问题出在 approach 而非 framing，可以做 major revision。
- 如果你认为 core problem 本身就有问题（gap 不存在、问题不够重要），pivot 到同一研究领域下的新方向可能是更好的选择。
- 当然，如果你有信心这一轮修订能实现突破，继续改进也完全可以。

最终由你判断——做你认为最能提升 idea 质量的选择。

## PC-LDCD: Probabilistic Circuits for Hallucination Detection

PC-LDCD (Probabilistic Circuit Latent Density Contrastive Decoding) is a method that intervenes only when the latent geometry deviates from factual regions, while leaving correct generations untouched.

### Addressing LLM Overconfidence

The research acknowledges a key limitation in existing hallucination detection approaches: Early approaches exploit token probability and semantic entropy, but suffer from LLM overconfidence and require multi-pass sampling. This is a critical problem because traditional uncertainty measures fail completely when LLMs produce high-confidence hallucinations where the model consistently generates the same incorrect output with high certainty, and entropy remains low because the model's probability distribution is sharply peaked around wrong answers.

### How PC-LDCD Works

PCNet, a Probabilistic Circuit trained as a tractable density estimator over a low-dimensional projection of the LLM's final hidden state, computes the exact Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) of any latent state in a single forward pass: no sampling, no external verifiers, and no weight modifications are needed. A high NLL identifies a hallucination trajectory as a geometric anomaly drifting off the factual manifold, where the manifold is the region of activation space where truthful tokens tend to cluster.

### Performance and Remaining Limitations

PCNet achieves near-perfect hallucination detection across CoQA, SQuAD v2.0, and TriviaQA with AUROC reaching up to 99%, while PC-LDCD reduces the mean corruption rate to 53.7% and achieves a preservation rate of 79.3%. However, existing approaches still suffer from a main limitation: they apply corrections indiscriminately to every token, corrupting also the originally correct generations.

## What is Atomic Calibration?

Atomic calibration evaluates confidence calibration at a fine-grained level by decomposing long responses into individual factual claims. Unlike "macro calibration" (which assigns a single confidence score to an entire response), this approach assesses whether "each atomic claim's confidence aligns with its factuality."

## Uncertainty Language and FActScore

The paper does not explicitly discuss how hedging or uncertainty expressions interact with FActScore evaluation. The authors focus on factuality assessment using "GPT-4o to decompose responses into atomic facts" and verify them against Wikipedia and search results. The study concentrates on objective factuality rather than linguistic expressions of uncertainty.

## Atomic Fact Decomposition

There's no indication that hedging language affects how facts are decomposed or scored. The FActScore-based approach treats atomic facts as discrete, verifiable statements independent of qualifiers the model may include.

## Calibration Metrics

The paper employs four primary metrics:

1. **ECE (Expected Calibration Error)**: Measures alignment between predicted confidence and actual correctness
2. **Brier Score**: Calculates squared differences between predicted probabilities and outcomes
3. **AUROC**: Assesses ranking quality of confidence scores
4. **Spearman Correlation**: Evaluates rank correlation between confidence and factuality

Lower values indicate better calibration for ECE and Brier Score; higher values indicate better performance for AUROC and correlation.

# Key Findings on LLM Overconfidence

## Main Findings

The paper demonstrates widespread overconfidence across LLM families and sizes. Models frequently assign high confidence to incorrect answers. For instance, one leading LLM reported 93% confidence for an incorrect IEEE award recipient when the actual answer differed.

## Calibration Measurement

Calibration is assessed through **Expected Calibration Error (ECE)**, computed using empirical binning with 0.1-sized bins to measure misalignment between predicted confidence and actual correctness. The researchers employ "elicited self-reports" (0-100 confidence scores) rather than token-level probabilities, arguing this better captures task-level belief in RLHF-tuned systems.

## Validation and Agreement Data

The paper includes inter-annotator agreement validation. Researchers conducted human evaluation on 100 sampled responses with three independent annotators. Results showed **"Cohen's kappa [of] 0.82 for GPT-4o-mini, indicating substantial agreement"** between the LLM judge and human evaluators. This validates the reliability of their automated evaluation approach, though they acknowledge minor inconsistencies in ambiguous cases.

The study also reports complementary metrics: instances where distractors "helped" (improving accuracy) versus "harmed" (degrading accuracy) performance across models.

# CSS and the Specificity-Factuality Tradeoff

## How CSS Handles Hedging

CSS doesn't use traditional hedging language. Instead, it employs **semantic backoff**: each claim exists at three specificity levels (fine, coarse, or omitted). When support is weak, the system downgrades to coarser formulations rather than adding qualifiers like "possibly" or "may."

## Interaction with FActScore

The paper uses a claimwise evaluation protocol rather than FActScore's official metrics. For their evaluation, claims are assigned binary support labels. The key distinction: a coarse claim isn't "less factual"—it's simply making fewer commitments. A claim about "signing in Geneva" (coarse) versus "signing in Geneva in 1985" (fine) both remain factually accurate if evidence supports the coarser version.

## The Core Insight

The central finding addresses your question directly: making claims less specific doesn't inherently improve factuality—it **reduces unsupported commitments**. The paper states that calibrated CSS achieves "0.9865" support precision while maintaining "0.9381 specificity retention." This suggests the system preserves useful content while eliminating unjustified detail.

The tradeoff insight is that "answer-level accuracy is often the wrong object" for evaluation. Instead, systems should answer "only as much as" evidence supports, creating a structured uncertainty layer where downstream components can escalate downgraded claims for re-verification or human review.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about "Simple Factuality Probes" and hallucination detection work. Here are the key findings:

## Simple Factuality Probes for Hallucination Detection

The "Simple Factuality Probes Detect Hallucinations in Long-Form Natural Language Generation" paper presents a simple baseline for detecting hallucinations in long-form LLM generations, with performance comparable to expensive multi-sample approaches while drawing only a single sample from the LLM generator.

The approach decomposes long-form generation into atomic claims, obtains hidden states for each claim using either the frontier LLM or a smaller LM, and applies a lightweight probe on hidden states to estimate claim-level factuality, attributing atomic claims to token spans and propagating claim-level factuality back to the long-form generation.

### Key Technical Findings

The work identifies a subset of neurons predominantly responsible for encoding common factuality, locates neuron activations such that supported and unsupported claims can be linearly separated by some threshold, and uses only sparse neuron activations to train probes performing comparably well.

Probes trained only on selected neuron activations (sparse probes) have comparable validation AUROC as compared with full-neuron probes trained with high sparsity constraints.

### Cross-Model Transfer and Performance

In hallucination detection benchmarks, lightweight probes achieve up to 13-point AUROC gains on 10 of 12 model–dataset combinations (LLaMA-2, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3 × four QA benchmarks).

The paper was published in Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2025, pages 16209–16226, in Suzhou, China.

# Models Tested and VUF Effectiveness

## Models Evaluated
The research tested three models: "Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct."

## Differential Sensitivity to VUF Intervention

The VUF direction demonstrated notably different effectiveness across models. When steering activations along the VUF, Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral showed strong responsiveness to intervention intensity changes. However, "Qwen2.5 exhibits a similar trend, it is significantly less sensitive compared to Llama3.1 and Mistral."

## Intervention Methodology

Researchers modified hidden states through linear addition: activations were adjusted by adding scaled VUF vectors (h^(l)(x) ← h^(l)(x) + α·r_VU^(l)), where α controlled intervention strength.

## Results Summary

**Hallucination Reduction (Average across datasets):**
- Llama: 32.4% → 22.3% (31.9% relative reduction)
- Mistral: 46.9% → 29.1%
- Qwen: 48.1% → 34.6%

**Calibration Improvements:**
For Llama on TriviaQA, the correlation between semantic and verbal uncertainty increased from 0.59 to 0.63, demonstrating improved alignment.

## Model-Specific Variation

Yes, substantial variation existed. The paper notes "Qwen2.5 is significantly less sensitive" to VUF interventions, suggesting architectural differences affect how representations encode uncertainty expression across these model families.

The paper establishes that "factual precision...measures the extent to which the factual claims made in G_o are supported by external evidence," while "factual recall...measures the extent to which G_o covers the facts that are salient and relevant." These are complementary but distinct metrics.

**Key Finding on the Trade-off:**
The research reveals a significant imbalance: "current LLMs perform substantially better on precision than on recall," indicating models excel at supporting individual claims but fail to cover comprehensive relevant information.

**Hedging and Specificity:**
The paper does not explicitly analyze how hedging or claim abstention affects precision scores. However, it notes that "not supported claims constitute the largest category," suggesting models generate many unverified statements rather than strategically avoiding claims.

The analysis shows "longer generations are neither necessary nor sufficient for better factuality." The paper tracks the "claim to fact ratio" to distinguish whether models inflate precision by simply generating more content. Results indicate some models achieve "near-maximum recall with substantially lower ratios," suggesting genuine efficiency rather than hedging strategies artificially boosting precision.

## The Three-Way Relationship

The paper establishes that hallucination rates depend on two primary factors according to the Kalai-Vempala theoretical framework. A "monofact" is "the fraction of facts seen exactly once" during training. The research shows these rare facts correlate directly with hallucination likelihood.

The paper defines miscalibration using total-variation distance between the model's probability distribution and the true data distribution, organized into logarithmic probability bins. The researchers measure this as "the sum of within-bin total-variation distances."
